body:
Glaciers as agents of landform development

A glacier is a large, persistent mass of ice formed on land from accumulated snow that moves under the influence of gravity. Glaciers are important agents of erosion, transportation and deposition, particularly in polar regions and high mountain environments.

Although glaciers move much more slowly than rivers, their enormous weight and the rock fragments embedded within them enable them to erode even resistant bedrock. Their activity produces distinctive valleys, mountain peaks, lakes and deposits.

Formation and movement of glaciers

Glaciers develop where snowfall accumulates over successive years because the snow gained exceeds the snow lost. Older snow becomes compacted under the weight of newer layers. It gradually changes into granular, partly compacted snow called firn, which eventually becomes dense glacial ice.

Gravity causes this ice to move. Movement occurs through internal deformation of the ice and, where conditions permit, sliding over the underlying bedrock.

Unlike seasonal snow, a glacier persists over several years and possesses the ability to flow. Unlike sea ice, which forms through the freezing of seawater, glacial ice originates from accumulated snow on land.

Major types of glaciers

TypeCharacteristicsExamples or setting
Mountain or valley glacierFlows along mountain slopes and valleysHimalayas and Alps
Continental ice sheetExtensive ice mass covering large land areasGreenland and Antarctica
Piedmont glacierForms when valley glaciers emerge from mountains and spread over relatively flat landPlains at mountain foothills

The Gangotri Glacier in Uttarakhand is an example of a Himalayan valley glacier. Its lower end, known as Gaumukh, supplies meltwater to the Bhagirathi River.

Glacier mass balance

Glacier mass balance is the difference between the mass gained by a glacier through accumulation and the mass lost through ablation during a specified period.

Accumulation

Accumulation adds mass to a glacier. Snowfall is its principal source, although avalanches, windblown snow and refreezing water may also contribute. In mountain glaciers, accumulation generally dominates at higher elevations.

Ablation

Ablation removes mass from a glacier through processes such as melting, sublimation and calving. Sublimation converts ice directly into water vapour. Calving occurs when pieces of ice break away from a glacier into a water body.

Ablation generally dominates at lower elevations, where temperatures are higher.

Equilibrium line

The equilibrium line separates the accumulation area from the ablation area. At this boundary, the local annual gain and loss of glacier mass are equal. Its elevation is called the equilibrium line altitude.

Warmer conditions or reduced snowfall can raise the equilibrium line, decreasing the proportion of the glacier in the accumulation zone. The equilibrium line is not necessarily identical to the permanent snowline.

Mass balanceConditionGeneral effect
PositiveAccumulation exceeds ablationGlacier gains mass
NegativeAblation exceeds accumulationGlacier loses mass
ZeroAccumulation equals ablationNo net mass change during the period

Glacial retreat does not mean backward ice flow

A retreating glacier may continue to flow downhill while its terminus moves uphill. Retreat occurs when ice is lost from the lower end faster than glacier movement replenishes it. Changes in glacier length may also lag behind changes in mass balance.

Prelims focus

  • Glaciers originate from accumulated snow on land and move primarily under gravity.
  • Firn is an intermediate stage between snow and glacial ice.
  • Greenland and Antarctica contain continental ice sheets.
  • Negative mass balance occurs when ablation exceeds accumulation.
  • The equilibrium line separates the accumulation and ablation zones.
  • Trap: Glacier retreat does not require the ice to flow backwards.

[References: NCERT, The Earth Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, Glaciers, printed pp. 66–67, online copy; National Snow and Ice Data Center, Science of Glaciers and Cryosphere Glossary: Equilibrium Line, consulted 28 November 2026. Source coverage: the relevant pages of project Volume 13 were unreadable, including the GCERT Landforms chapter, and Volume 14 was unavailable; the accessible project textbooks and corresponding online NCERT material were used instead.]

title: Glaciers: Formation, Movement and Mass Balance

body:
How glaciers erode the landscape

Glacial erosion occurs mainly through plucking and abrasion. These processes enable moving ice to enlarge existing valleys, excavate depressions and reshape mountain ridges.

  • Plucking: Water enters fractures in bedrock and may freeze around loosened rock fragments. Moving ice incorporates these fragments and carries them away.
  • Abrasion: Rock fragments embedded in moving ice scrape, grind and polish the underlying bedrock.

Abrasion may produce parallel scratches called glacial striations. Their alignment provides evidence of the direction in which ice formerly moved.

Mountain peaks and ridges

Cirque, corrie or cwm

A cirque is a deep, bowl-shaped depression at the head of a glacial valley. It typically has steep surrounding walls and an excavated floor. Snow and ice accumulate within the depression, and continued glacial erosion enlarges it.

After the glacier melts, water may occupy the depression, forming a small lake called a tarn or cirque lake.

Arete

When glaciers erode adjacent valleys or cirques from opposite sides, the intervening ridge becomes progressively narrower. The resulting sharp, steep-sided ridge is called an arete.

Horn

When 3 or more cirques erode towards a common mountain summit from different directions, they may leave a sharply pointed, pyramidal peak called a horn. The Matterhorn in the Alps is a classic example.

Col

A col is a saddle-shaped depression or mountain pass between higher peaks. Glacial erosion can lower a section of an intervening ridge and produce such a pass.

Glacial valleys

U-shaped valley

A mountain glacier commonly occupies a valley originally formed by running water. Its broad mass of moving ice erodes both the valley floor and sides. Over time, the original valley may develop a broad floor and steep sides, creating a U-shaped cross-section.

FeatureRiver valleyGlacial valley
Typical cross-sectionV-shaped, especially in mountain coursesU-shaped
Principal agentRunning waterMoving ice
Typical valley floorRelatively narrow in a youthful mountain valleyRelatively broad

Hanging valley

A large main glacier usually erodes its valley more deeply than a smaller tributary glacier. After the ice disappears, the tributary valley may remain suspended above the floor of the main valley. Streams flowing from such hanging valleys often form waterfalls.

Truncated spurs

A river may wind around projecting ridges known as interlocking spurs. A large glacier can cut through these projections, leaving steep, triangular rock faces called truncated spurs.

Fjords and other evidence of glaciation

A fjord is a deep, narrow coastal inlet formed when seawater occupies a glacially excavated valley. Fjords generally have steep sides and may extend considerably below sea level. Norway is particularly famous for its fjord coastline.

A fjord is therefore primarily a glacial erosional feature subsequently flooded by the sea, rather than a valley originally excavated by marine waves.

A roche moutonnee is a bedrock hill modified by glacier movement. Its upstream side is generally smoother and more gently inclined because of abrasion, while its downstream side is steeper and rougher because of plucking.

These landforms can survive long after the glaciers that produced them have disappeared, providing evidence of past climatic conditions and former glaciation.

Prelims focus

  • Cirque is a bowl-shaped erosional depression; a tarn is a lake occupying it.
  • Aretes are sharp ridges between adjacent glacially eroded areas.
  • Horns develop through erosion from 3 or more sides.
  • Hanging valleys result from unequal erosion by main and tributary glaciers.
  • Fjords are seawater-filled glacial valleys.
  • Trap: A roche moutonnee is eroded bedrock, whereas a drumlin is a streamlined landform associated with deposition and reshaping of glacial sediments.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 3, Work of Ice; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, printed pp. 66–68 and Figure 7.13, online copy; U.S. National Park Service, Glacier Landforms series, consulted 28 November 2026.]

body:
Transportation and deposition by glaciers

Glaciers carry material ranging from fine rock powder to large boulders. Rock debris may travel on the surface, within the ice or underneath the glacier. When ice melts or releases its load, the transported material is deposited.

The nature of the resulting deposit depends on whether the material was deposited directly by ice or transported and deposited by meltwater.

Glacial till and outwash

CharacteristicGlacial tillGlaciofluvial outwash
Depositing agentGlacial iceGlacial meltwater
SortingGenerally poorly sortedRelatively well sorted
LayeringUsually unstratifiedCommonly stratified
Rock fragmentsOften angular or subangularFrequently more rounded

The difference arises because glaciers can carry fine particles and enormous boulders together. Flowing meltwater, however, tends to separate material according to particle size and its ability to transport the load.

Moraines

A moraine is an accumulation of glacial debris, often appearing as a ridge or irregular blanket. Different types of moraines are identified according to their position relative to the glacier.

  • Lateral moraine: A ridge of debris along the side of a glacier.
  • Medial moraine: A debris ridge along the middle of a glacier, commonly formed when adjacent lateral moraines combine as 2 glaciers merge.
  • Terminal moraine: A ridge deposited at or near the furthest position reached during a particular glacial advance.
  • Recessional moraine: A ridge formed at a temporary stationary or readvancing position during the overall retreat of a glacier.
  • Ground moraine: An irregular sheet or blanket of till deposited beneath the glacier or left across the ground after melting.

Terminal and recessional moraines are valuable indicators of former glacier margins. Moraine ridges may also obstruct drainage and create glacial lakes.

Other depositional features

Drumlins

Drumlins are elongated, streamlined hills formed beneath moving glaciers, commonly composed of till and sometimes other sediments. A typical drumlin has a relatively blunt, steeper end facing the direction from which the glacier came and a narrower, gently tapering end pointing down-ice.

Groups of drumlins may occur together, producing a landscape sometimes described as basket-of-eggs topography. Their long axes generally indicate former ice-flow directions.

Eskers

An esker is a long, narrow and winding ridge of sand and gravel deposited by meltwater flowing through channels beneath or within a glacier. When the surrounding ice melts, the sediment-filled channel remains as a raised ridge.

Outwash plains

Outwash plains are broad depositional surfaces formed beyond glacier margins by meltwater streams. They consist mainly of sorted sand and gravel, often deposited by branching or braided streams.

Glacial erratics

A glacial erratic is a rock fragment transported by a glacier and deposited away from its original source. It may differ considerably in composition from the local bedrock. Erratics provide evidence of former ice transport.

Kettles and kettle lakes

Blocks of detached glacial ice may become buried in sediment. When the buried ice melts, the overlying surface subsides and leaves a depression called a kettle. If the depression fills with water, it becomes a kettle lake.

Do not confuse glacial lakes

A tarn occupies a depression excavated by glacial erosion, a kettle lake forms after the melting of buried ice, and a moraine-dammed lake develops when deposited debris obstructs drainage.

Prelims focus

  • Glacial till is generally unsorted; outwash is sorted and stratified.
  • Medial moraines commonly form when 2 valley glaciers merge.
  • Terminal moraines mark former limits of glacier advance.
  • Drumlins are streamlined hills aligned with former ice movement.
  • Eskers are winding ridges deposited by glacial meltwater.
  • Trap: Eskers are not ridges excavated directly into bedrock by glacial erosion.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 3, Work of Ice; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 7, printed pp. 68–69 and Figure 7.14, online copy; U.S. National Park Service, Glacier Landforms series and Outwash Plains and Eskers, consulted 28 November 2026.]
